title: Haughty Eyes
excerpt: Pride tops the list of things the LORD hates, and it's the sin we're least likely to see in ourselves. Proverbs on pride, and the humility of Jesus.

blocks.text: Let me guess how you're reading this.

You're probably nodding along, thinking of someone you know who really needs to hear it. A coworker who can't admit a mistake. A relative who always has to be right. A public figure whose ego is out of control. Pride is such an obvious problem in *them.*
And that's exactly the problem. Pride is the only sin that gets worse the more certain you are that you don't have it.
Keep that in mind as we read what Proverbs says, because the writer isn't gentle about this one.
First on the List

verses: There are six things the LORD hates, seven that are detestable to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood...

blocks.text: Read the list again and pay attention to the order. Before lying. Before violence. Before the schemes of a wicked heart, the lead item is *haughty eyes.* A look. A posture. A way of seeing yourself above other people.

Why would God put that at the front? Most of us would rank murder well above an attitude. But Proverbs seems to see pride as the root the other sins grow from. Think about it. Lying often starts with protecting an image. Violence often starts with wounded ego. Cruelty, gossip, and refusing to forgive all trace back to one quiet sentence: *I matter more than you.*
Pride is the original sin in more ways than one. It was the first temptation: "you will be like God" (Genesis 3:5). And it still is.
Where Pride Hides
The reason pride is so dangerous is that it rarely looks like pride from the inside. It disguises itself.

It looks like **confidence.** It looks like *being right.* It looks like **high standards,** like **strength,** like **never needing help.** It can even look like **humility,** the person who constantly talks themselves down so you'll reassure them, which is still entirely about themselves.
So here are a few symptoms, and you can check them against your own life.

items: **You can't say "I was wrong."** Not "I'm sorry you feel that way." Not "mistakes were made." Just: *I was wrong.* If that sentence sticks in your throat, pay attention.
**You can't be corrected.** When someone points out a flaw, your first reaction is defense, not curiosity. You have an explanation ready before they've finished the sentence.
**You keep score.** You know exactly who owes you an apology, who didn't thank you, and how much more you've given than they have.
**You quietly believe you'd handle it better.** Their parenting, their marriage, their job, their ministry. You'd never say it out loud, but the thought is always there.
**You can't ask for help.** Needing someone feels like losing.
**You look down.** At people who've made different choices, who aren't as disciplined, as informed, as spiritual as you.

blocks.text: If you found yourself in two or three of those, you're in good company. I found myself in most of them.
"More Hope for a Fool"
Now we get to the sentence that I think is one of the harshest in the whole book:

verses: Do you see a person wise in their own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for them.

blocks.text: Stop and absorb that. In Proverbs, the *fool* is about as low as it gets. He's the one who ignores wisdom, repeats his mistakes, and ruins his own life. And yet the book says there is more hope for him than for the person who thinks they already have it figured out.

Why? Because a fool can still be taught. If he ever wakes up and realizes he doesn't know what he's doing, the door is open. But the person who's convinced they're already wise has nothing left to learn. They've closed the one door that leads out. You can't help someone who doesn't think they need it.
It's worth noticing who Jesus reserved His sharpest words for. Not the prostitutes or tax collectors. The people who were *sure* they were righteous.
The Prayer That Sounded Perfect

He told a story about this. Two men went up to the temple to pray (Luke 18:9–14). One was a Pharisee, a deeply religious man, respected and disciplined. The other was a tax collector, widely despised.

The Pharisee stood and prayed: "God, I thank you that I am not like other people — robbers, evildoers, adulterers — or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week and give a tenth of all I get."

Read it carefully. It sounds like a prayer. It begins with thanks. It's full of good things: he fasts, he tithes, he stays away from obvious sin. And yet Jesus says it never made it past the ceiling. Because the whole prayer was a performance, a comparison, a way of standing taller than the man next to him. Pride dressed up as gratitude.
Meanwhile, the tax collector wouldn't even lift his eyes. He beat his chest and said just seven words: "God, have mercy on me, a sinner."
And Jesus says *that* man went home right with God. Not the one with the resume. The one with empty hands.
What Pride Costs

Proverbs doesn't leave this abstract. "Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall" (16:18). "Pride brings a person low, but the lowly in spirit gain honor" (29:23). And elsewhere: "Where there is strife, there is pride" (13:10). Look at the last time a relationship exploded. Chances are, somewhere in the middle of it, two people each refused to be the first to say sorry.

The Bible's history is full of proud people who were brought low. King Nebuchadnezzar stood on his palace roof and boasted, "Is not this the great Babylon I have built... by my mighty power and for the glory of my majesty?" (Daniel 4:30). Within the hour, he lost his mind and lived like an animal for years. When he finally recovered, the first thing he did was lift his eyes to heaven and praise God, and confess that "those who walk in pride he is able to humble" (4:37).

God isn't being petty. He's being merciful. Pride is a lie about who we are, and left alone it leads somewhere terrible. Sometimes the kindest thing He can do is to take away what we've been leaning on.

And listen to what the other half of the promise says: "He mocks proud mockers but shows favor to the humble and oppressed" (3:34). The New Testament repeats it twice (James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5): "God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble."
Think about that. *God opposes the proud.* Not just disapproves. Opposes. Whoever you've been trying to impress, whatever you've been trying to prove, you don't want to be on the wrong side of that.
The One Who Had Every Right

If humility were just about thinking less of yourself, it would be miserable. It isn't. It's seeing yourself accurately, as someone deeply loved and deeply in need, and then forgetting yourself long enough to love others.

And the clearest picture of it is Jesus. Paul describes it in one of the most breathtaking passages in the Bible. Jesus, "being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he made himself nothing... he humbled himself by becoming obedient to death — even death on a cross!" (Philippians 2:6–8).

Think about who has the most right to be proud in all of history. The One who made the universe. The One who deserved worship, who could have demanded it. And He washed His disciples' feet. He was slapped, mocked, and spat on, and He didn't defend Himself. Next to Him, every one of our reasons for pride starts to look small.

Here's the good news. You don't have to defend your image anymore. You don't have to be right all the time, or the best at everything, or impressive. The tax collector's seven words are enough. *God, have mercy on me, a sinner.* The One who humbled Himself for you is ready to lift you up, because He loves you.

So look at your own eyes today. Where have they been looking down? Where have you been defending, comparing, keeping score? And what would it look like to lower them, just a little, and let God be God?

items: Which of the symptoms felt most uncomfortably familiar? Can't apologize, can't be corrected, keeping score, looking down on others, or refusing help. What is one specific situation where pride might be quietly running things right now?
When was the last time you said "I was wrong" and meant it? Is there someone you owe an apology to, someone you've been waiting for to go first? What would it look like to be the one who goes first?

Are you more like the Pharisee or the tax collector in how you come to God? Do you come with a list of what you've done, or with empty hands? What would it look like to pray those seven words honestly today?

blocks.text: Lord, I'm sorry for the ways I've exalted myself and looked down on others. Search me and show me where pride is hiding, in my defensiveness, my comparisons, my need to be right. Give me the humility of Jesus, who made Himself nothing for my sake. Teach me to receive correction, to say sorry first, and to come to You with empty hands. God, have mercy on me, a sinner. Amen.
